The telharmonium was an early American electric organ, an electrophone and electromechanical instrument, H-S 52. It generated pitch signals with tone wheels and an alternator, transmitted them over the telephone line, and sounded at the receiving end through horn loudspeakers. The player sat at a console and, with organ-like keyboards, stops and pedals, mixed harmonics and changed the timbre and the volume, and could imitate the flute, bassoon, clarinet and cello. Thaddeus Cahill played music on it to telephone subscribers and to live audiences in New York City; Lee DeForest also broadcast wirelessly with it from Telharmonic Hall.
泰爾哈莫尼琴為電鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs編號52。來源未載明琴身: The telharmonium was an electrophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 52. The source does not state the materials of the body, the keyboards or the tone wheels; it records only that the sounding body consists of toothed wheels and brushes and that a large generator supplied the current. At the receiving end a metal cone was attached to the mouthpiece to form a primitive loudspeaker; there was also a large paper cone output, and the source mentions an electromagnetic diaphragm as the better output part. The materials of the rest are not recorded.
泰爾哈莫尼琴由 Thaddeus Cahill 約一八九六年發展、一八九七年取得: The telharmonium was developed by Thaddeus Cahill around 1896 and patented in 1897; it was an early electric organ. He imagined transmitting music over the telephone line, with the sound coming from a metal cone at the receiving end. Three versions were built: the 1901 prototype had only eight alternators; the second, of 1906, weighed nearly two hundred tons and needed two players, and was tried as a subscription service, which Bell Telephone refused, and Lee DeForest broadcast it by radio; the third, of 1911, was installed in New York. Because of its size, its power consumption and crosstalk, the company failed in 1914, and the instrument was broken up in 1962.
